trade: Civics class at the civic centre's meeting chamber — learner and teacher
header: Lower- and upper-secondary civics, generic: how a public council meeting runs, how a resident gets heard in public comment, and how a decision is recorded — no real council, place or person.
name: How a Local Council Meeting Works
tagline: Read the agenda, sign up to speak, keep to your point, and check what the minutes record

badge.name: Heard in Public
badge.note: An agenda read, a clear public comment given and the decision checked in the minutes

hazards.label: Stand up and speak without signing up?
hazards.text: You stood up to speak without signing up. Public meetings run public comment by their own procedure, usually a sign-up with the clerk, so everyone gets a fair turn; speaking out of turn usually means not being heard at all.

hazards.label: Criticise a council member personally?
hazards.text: You attacked a council member personally. Public comment is most effective when it is about the issue and what you want done; a personal attack gives people a reason to stop listening and often breaks the meeting's own conduct rules.

hazards.label: Quote a figure you heard somewhere?
hazards.text: You quoted a figure you could not source. In public comment, a claim you cannot back up weakens everything else you say; say what you have seen yourself, or say where the information comes from.

hazards.label: Rely on what you remember was decided?
hazards.text: You relied on what you remembered was decided. The official record of a meeting is its minutes; checking them is how residents confirm what was actually agreed and hold the council to it.

find1.title: Find the parts of the meeting
find1.cue: Mark the three documents and stations every public meeting in this lesson uses.
find1.why: A public meeting runs on three things residents can use: the agenda that lists what will be discussed, the sign-up sheet for public comment and the minutes that record what was decided. Knowing where each is lets anyone take part, not just people who have been before. The council here is generic, not any real one.
items: What will be discussed, in order. Read it before the meeting.
How a resident gets a turn to speak.
the minutes of the last meeting
The official record of what was decided.
decoy: Part of the room, not part of taking part. Look for the agenda, sign-up and minutes.

select1.title: Read the agenda before the meeting
select1.cue: Find the item you care about on the agenda and when it comes up.
select1.why: Reading the agenda tells you whether the issue you care about is being discussed and roughly when. Public comment on the item under discussion is heard at the right moment; turning up without reading it means missing your chance.
select1.label: Read the agenda first

seq.title: Put the public comment in order
seq.cue: Your name and where you live, the item, your point, what you ask for.
seq.why: An effective public comment is short and in a clear order: who you are, which item you are speaking on, the point you want to make and what you are asking the council to do. The order helps the council, the clerk and the other residents follow you.
seq.oon: Out of order. Say who you are and which item before your point, so people know what you are talking about.

hold.title: Listen to the discussion before you speak
hold.cue: Hold still and listen to the council's discussion of the item.
hold.why: Listening to the discussion first tells you what has already been said and what the council is unsure about. A comment that answers a real question in the room is far more useful than one that repeats what everyone has heard.
hold.brk: You stopped listening and started rehearsing. Listen to what is actually being said.
hold.label: Listening to the debate

turn.title: Turn from observer to speaker
turn.cue: Your name is called. Turn from listening to speaking.
turn.why: Moving from observer to speaker is the step most residents never take. Doing it calmly, when your name is called and not before, is what the procedure is for: it gives every resident the same fair turn. Signing up in advance also lets the chair plan the time so that nobody who came to speak is left out.
turn.label: Observer to speaker

gauge.title: Speak at a clear, steady pace
gauge.cue: Commit when your pace is clear enough to follow — not rushed, not dragging.
gauge.why: Public comment is usually short, which tempts people to rush. A clear, steady pace makes sure the council and the clerk actually catch your point; a rushed one loses it. Practising the comment aloud beforehand is the easiest way to find the pace that fits the time allowed.
gauge.label: Speaking pace
gauge.miss: Outside the band. Too fast and nobody catches your point; too slow and you run out of turn. Try again.

drag.title: Hand your written comment to the clerk
drag.cue: Drag your written comment to the clerk so it can be entered in the record.
drag.why: Handing a written version to the clerk means your point is recorded accurately, even if the minutes summarise the spoken comments. It is a simple step that makes a public comment last beyond the meeting. A written copy also helps the clerk record your point accurately in the minutes.
drag.label: Your written comment
drag.miss: Not in place yet. Take it all the way to with the clerk.

select2.title: Keep it about the issue
select2.cue: Make your point about the issue and what should be done, not about a person.
select2.why: Comments about the issue are heard; comments about a person are resisted. Keeping to the issue and what you want done is both more respectful and more effective, and it is what most meetings' conduct rules ask for. Speaking to the chair keeps the exchange about the issue rather than about the people in the room.
select2.label: The issue, not the person

find2.title: Spot the problems in a classmate's comment
find2.cue: Look at the draft public comment and mark each problem.
find2.why: Public comments go wrong in predictable ways: no clear ask, a personal attack and a claim with no source. Spotting them in a draft is how you learn to write a comment that gets heard. The usual problems are the same every time: wandering off the item, running long and leaving out the ask.
items: What do you want the council to do? Say it.
Keep to the issue. Attacks stop people listening.
Say what you saw yourself or where it comes from.
decoy: Naming the item helps everyone follow. Keep it.

track.title: Stay calm while others disagree
track.cue: Hold your composure in band as another resident speaks against your point.
track.why: Hearing someone disagree in public is uncomfortable. Staying calm, listening and not interrupting is what lets the meeting work for everyone, including you, the next time you speak. Meetings run on everyone following the same rules, and a resident who does is listened to more readily.
track.brk: You lost your composure. Breathe, listen and let them finish.
track.label: Calm in the chamber

record.title: Check the decision in the minutes
record.cue: When the minutes are published, check what was recorded as decided.
record.why: The minutes are the official record. Checking them confirms what was actually decided and whether your comment was noted, and it is how residents follow up and hold a council to its decisions. Without checking the minutes, a resident can leave believing something was agreed that never actually was.
record.label: Check the minutes

share.title: Explain the process to the class
share.cue: Explain how a resident gets heard, from the agenda to the minutes.
share.why: Explaining the process from agenda to minutes turns a single visit into something the whole class can use. Many adults never learn it; knowing it is a real civic skill. Knowing how the meeting works means you can take part in decisions about your own street, school or park.
share.label: Share with the class

checkin.title: Check in at the end of the lesson
checkin.cue: How did the meeting go? What question do you still have?
checkin.why: A short check-in lets the teacher hear what made sense and what did not, and gives each learner a moment to name one question they still have. Nobody is graded here, and a teacher or trusted adult is there for anyone who wants to talk more.
checkin.label: End-of-lesson check-in

interrupts.label: Tell the clerk and call for help
interrupts.alert: A resident near you says they feel faint and sits down heavily.
interrupts.cue: Tell the clerk straight away so help is called; do not try to treat them yourself.
interrupts.why: When someone is unwell at a meeting, the right response is to get help quickly: tell the clerk, who can pause the meeting and call for help. It is never a learner's job to treat anyone.
interrupts.miss: Nobody told the clerk, and help was called late. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.
interrupts.wrong: That does not get help. Tell the clerk. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Clerk told and help called. The meeting paused, then resumed.

interrupts.label: Name the agenda item
interrupts.alert: The clerk asks which agenda item you signed up to speak on.
interrupts.cue: Name the item from the agenda.
interrupts.why: The clerk runs public comment item by item. Naming your item means you are called at the right moment and your comment is recorded against the right decision.
interrupts.miss: You could not name the item, and your turn passed. Next time, stop the lesson and deal with it first.
interrupts.wrong: That does not name the item. Give the agenda item. Choose the response that deals with it now.
interrupts.done: Item named. You will be called when it comes up.

guide.hazard: Stop. Check how this meeting's own rules say it is done.

lateRecord: The minutes are checked after they are published — nothing to check yet.
lateCheckin: The check-in comes at the very end of the lesson.
